title: Join Simple Ideas with og, men, eller, for, and så
goal: Use five common Norwegian joining words to connect words and simple clauses.

objectives.statement: Use five common Norwegian joining words to connect words and simple clauses.

spans.value: Mina and Jonas are deciding what to do on Saturday. They want to spend time together, but the weather may affect their plans.
Hva vil du gjøre på lørdag?

blocks.translation: What do you want to do on Saturday?

spans.value: Jeg vil gå en tur og spise lunsj ute.

blocks.translation: I want to go for a walk and eat lunch out.

spans.value: Det høres hyggelig ut, men det skal regne.

blocks.translation: That sounds nice, but it is going to rain.

spans.value: Skal vi gå på kafé eller lage mat hjemme?

blocks.translation: Shall we go to a café or cook at home?

spans.value: Vi kan gå på kafé, for jeg har lyst på kake.

blocks.translation: We can go to a café, because I feel like having cake.

spans.value: Flott! Kafeen åpner klokka ti, så vi kan møtes halv elleve.

blocks.translation: Great! The café opens at ten, so we can meet at half past ten.

spans.value: Ja, og etterpå kan vi gå en kort tur.

blocks.translation: Yes, and afterwards we can go for a short walk.

spans.value: The conversation moves forward through a series of small connections. Jonas combines two activities. Mina introduces a contrast. Jonas presents a choice. Mina gives a reason. Finally, Jonas draws a practical conclusion.
The five joining words doing this work are:
These words are called coordinating conjunctions (
). They connect words or simple clauses that have a similar role in the sentence. A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a verb, such as
The important choice is not only which English translation looks familiar. You must decide what relationship you want to express: addition, contrast, choice, reason, or result.
when both connected ideas belong together. It often corresponds directly to English

no.value: Mina bestiller kaffe og kake.

en.value: Mina orders coffee and cake.

no.value: Kafeen er liten og koselig.

en.value: The café is small and cosy.

no.value: Jonas går en tur og spiser lunsj ute.

en.value: Jonas goes for a walk and eats lunch out.

spans.value: Here Jonas performs both actions. Because the subject is the same, Norwegian does not need to repeat
You can also connect two complete clauses:

no.value: Mina bestiller kaffe, og Jonas bestiller te.

en.value: Mina orders coffee, and Jonas orders tea.

spans.value: Each part has its own subject and verb:

no.value: Mina bestiller kaffe.

en.value: Mina orders coffee.

no.value: Jonas bestiller te.

en.value: Jonas orders tea.

statement.value: when you want to add one word, action, or simple idea to another.

spans.value: A common mistake is to treat
as if it means “and then” in every sentence. It can show that two things both happen, but it does not automatically emphasize a result.

no.value: Jeg kjøper brød og lager lunsj.

en.value: I buy bread and make lunch.

no.value: Jeg har ikke brød, så jeg går til butikken.

en.value: I do not have bread, so I go to the shop.

spans.value: The first sentence adds two actions. The second says that one fact leads to another.
when the second idea contrasts with the first. English normally uses
In the dialogue, Mina agrees that Jonas’s idea sounds pleasant, but she introduces a problem:

no.value: Det høres hyggelig ut, men det skal regne.

en.value: That sounds nice, but it is going to rain.

spans.value: The rain does not cancel the pleasant idea completely. It changes how Mina and Jonas must think about it.

no.value: Kafeen er liten, men den er populær.

en.value: The café is small, but it is popular.

no.value: Jeg liker kaffe, men jeg drikker te i dag.

en.value: I like coffee, but I am drinking tea today.

no.value: Jonas vil gå en lang tur, men Mina vil gå en kort tur.

en.value: Jonas wants to go for a long walk, but Mina wants to go for a short walk.

spans.value: You can also connect shorter elements:

no.value: Kaken er god, men dyr.

en.value: The cake is good but expensive.

statement.value: when the second word or idea is different from what the first one might lead you to expect.

no.value: Kafeen er liten og koselig.

en.value: The café is small and cosy.

no.value: Kafeen er liten, men koselig.

en.value: The café is small but cosy.

spans.value: are simply two descriptions. In the second, the speaker suggests that being small could be a disadvantage, yet the café is cosy.
A common mistake is to use
merely because both ideas are true. The relationship between them matters more than the fact that both appear in the same sentence.

no.value: Jeg er trøtt, men jeg går på jobb.

en.value: I am tired, but I am going to work.

spans.value: Both statements are true, but the second contrasts with the expectation created by the first.
to connect alternatives. It corresponds to English

no.value: Skal vi gå på kafé eller lage mat hjemme?

en.value: Shall we go to a café or cook at home?

spans.value: . Mina and Jonas are deciding between them.

no.value: Vil du ha kaffe eller te?

en.value: Would you like coffee or tea?

no.value: Er kafeen åpen eller stengt?

en.value: Is the café open or closed?

no.value: Vi kan møtes klokka ti, eller vi kan møtes klokka elleve.

en.value: We can meet at ten, or we can meet at eleven.

spans.value: It is especially common in questions, but it also appears in statements:

no.value: På lørdag spiser vi på kafé eller hjemme.

en.value: On Saturday we will eat at a café or at home.

statement.value: when the connected words or ideas are alternatives.

no.value: Mina kjøper kaffe og kake.

en.value: Mina buys coffee and cake.

no.value: Mina kjøper kaffe eller kake.

en.value: Mina buys coffee or cake.

spans.value: A common mistake is to translate English
without checking whether the Norwegian sentence actually presents a choice. If both things happen, use
. If one possibility is set against another, use
when the second clause gives a reason for the first. In this use,

no.value: Vi kan gå på kafé, for jeg har lyst på kake.

en.value: We can go to a café, because I feel like having cake.

spans.value: The first clause gives the suggestion. The second clause explains why Mina makes it.

no.value: Jonas tar med en paraply, for det skal regne.

en.value: Jonas brings an umbrella because it is going to rain.

no.value: Vi går inn, for det er kaldt ute.

en.value: We go inside because it is cold outside.

no.value: Jeg bestiller te, for jeg liker ikke kaffe.

en.value: I order tea because I do not like coffee.

statement.value: The compact rule is: state the decision or situation first, then use

spans.value: A useful way to check the meaning is to ask “Why?”

no.value: Hvorfor tar Jonas med en paraply?

en.value: Why does Jonas bring an umbrella?

no.value: Han tar med en paraply, for det skal regne.

en.value: He brings an umbrella because it is going to rain.

spans.value: Do not confuse this conjunction with
. In this chapter, the target use of
connects a statement with its reason.
when the second clause is a consequence rather than an explanation.

no.value: Det regner, for himmelen er mørk.

en.value: It is raining, because the sky is dark.

spans.value: This is usually illogical: a dark sky does not normally cause or explain the fact that rain is falling. The speaker may instead mean that the dark sky is evidence, but that is not the simple reason relationship being practised here.

no.value: Vi tar med paraplyer, for det regner.

en.value: We are bringing umbrellas because it is raining.

spans.value: when the second clause is a result or consequence of the first. It corresponds to English

no.value: Kafeen åpner klokka ti, så vi kan møtes halv elleve.

en.value: The café opens at ten, so we can meet at half past ten.

spans.value: The opening time makes the meeting time possible. The first clause gives the situation; the second gives its result.

no.value: Det regner, så vi går på kafé.

en.value: It is raining, so we are going to a café.

no.value: Mina er sulten, så hun bestiller lunsj.

en.value: Mina is hungry, so she orders lunch.

no.value: Bussen er forsinket, så Jonas kommer sent.

en.value: The bus is delayed, so Jonas arrives late.

statement.value: The compact rule is: state a situation first, then use
to introduce what happens because of it.

no.value: Vi går på kafé, for det regner.

en.value: We are going to a café because it is raining.

no.value: Det regner, så vi går på kafé.

en.value: It is raining, so we are going to a café.

spans.value: The facts are similar, but the direction is different.
, the action comes first and the reason follows:
, the situation comes first and the result follows:

no.value: Jeg spiser lunsj, for jeg er sulten.

en.value: I am eating lunch because I am hungry.

no.value: Jeg er sulten, så jeg spiser lunsj.

en.value: I am hungry, so I am eating lunch.

spans.value: A common mistake is to choose between
only by translating an English sentence word for word. Instead, ask what comes second. If the second clause explains the first, use
. If the second clause follows as a result, use
All five joining words can appear between simple clauses, but the relationship changes.

no.value: Mina drikker kaffe, og Jonas drikker te.

en.value: Mina drinks coffee, and Jonas drinks tea.

no.value: Mina drikker kaffe, men Jonas drikker te.

en.value: Mina drinks coffee, but Jonas drinks tea.

spans.value: The drinks are presented as a contrast.

no.value: Mina drikker kaffe, eller Jonas drikker te.

en.value: Mina drinks coffee, or Jonas drinks tea.

spans.value: The sentence presents the clauses as alternatives.

no.value: Mina drikker kaffe, for hun er trøtt.

en.value: Mina drinks coffee because she is tired.

spans.value: The second clause gives Mina’s reason.

no.value: Mina er trøtt, så hun drikker kaffe.

en.value: Mina is tired, so she drinks coffee.

spans.value: The second clause gives the result.
When two complete clauses are connected in the patterns taught here, a comma is normally required at the boundary:

no.value: Det er kaldt, men vi sitter ute.

en.value: It is cold, but we are sitting outside.

no.value: Vi sitter inne, for det regner.

en.value: We are sitting inside because it is raining.

spans.value: Do not normally insert a comma when you are only connecting individual words:

no.value: Vi kjøper kaffe og kake.

en.value: We buy coffee and cake.

spans.value: Meaning remains the main focus. First choose the correct relationship; then write the joined sentence clearly.
On Saturday morning, Mina arrives first. Jonas sends her a message.
Bussen er forsinket, så jeg kommer litt sent.

blocks.translation: The bus is delayed, so I will be a little late.

spans.value: Det går bra, for jeg har en bok med meg.

blocks.translation: That is fine because I have a book with me.

spans.value: Vil du vente inne eller ute?

blocks.translation: Do you want to wait inside or outside?
I am sitting inside and reading.

spans.value: Det regner, men jeg har paraply.

blocks.translation: It is raining, but I have an umbrella.

spans.value: Fint! Jeg bestiller kaffe, og du kan bestille når du kommer.

blocks.translation: Good! I will order coffee, and you can order when you arrive.

spans.value: The same five words now help Mina and Jonas handle a changed situation. Notice how each connection has a distinct job:

items.value: Jonas offers two places to wait: choice.
The bus delay causes him to arrive late: result.
Mina explains why waiting is acceptable: reason.
Rain creates a problem, but the umbrella changes the expectation: contrast.

prompt.value: Read Lea’s message and reply in Norwegian. Confirm or adjust the dinner plan, explain your choices, and connect the details with «og», «men», «eller», «for», and «så».

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate criteria reply-purpose, explains-choices, uses-conjunctions as gating criteria; record og-addition-observation, men-contrast-observation, eller-choice-observation, for-reason-observation, and sa-result-observation diagnostically; observations must never make the response fail.

criteria.instruction: The reply is a Norwegian reply to Lea that confirms or adjusts the dinner plan.
The reply explains the choices, for example why the meal is at home or which time fits, using the supplied facts.
The reply links ideas with all five coordinating conjunctions og, men, eller, for, and så, each used accurately.
Observation only: note whether og expresses addition accurately; do not fail the reply on this observation.
Observation only: note whether men expresses contrast accurately; do not fail the reply on this observation.
Observation only: note whether eller presents alternatives accurately; do not fail the reply on this observation.
Observation only: note whether for introduces a logical reason accurately; do not fail the reply on this observation.
Observation only: note whether så introduces a logical result accurately; do not fail the reply on this observation.
